politica.por_que: Las 30 consultas de evaluación se trazan **completas** (el registro de decisiones). No son dato de un tercero: son obras de nuestro propio held-out, versionadas con el ground truth porque son el **instrumento de medición** (el registro de decisiones). Trazarlas enteras cumple las técnicas avanzadas aisladas por medición, la tabla de tokens, costo y la figura y el criterio de costo sin tocar el compromiso de privacidad.

entrada.nota_de_retencion: el registro de decisiones (cierra la pregunta por el ciclo de vida de la corrida purgada): **no se persiste nada de un tercero**. aic:147005.texto:
This thangka most likely depicts the Arhat Vanavasin. He is seated amidst mountains facing slightly right with a flywhisk in his left hand and his right making a pointing gesture, just as he is described in certain Tibetan liturgical verses. He is surrounded by lush green and blue foliage, and seated beneath a small floating image of White Tara above. Tara appears peaceful, seated on a lotus, with one face and two hands, and holds a lotus with her left hand while making the boon-granting gesture (varada mudra) with her right.
The Sixteen Arhats were legendary early Indian disciples of the Buddha Shakyamuni. Although they were not worshipped individually and emerged relatively late as an iconographic group, they became a popular subject in Buddhist art in both Tibet and East Asia. The complete group usually consists of twenty-five figures: the sixteen arhats, the Buddha Shakyamuni, his two attendants Shariputra and Maudgalyayana, the Chinese monk devotee Hvashang and the lay upasaka Dharmatala, and the Four Great King of the cardinal directions, Dhritarashtra, Virudhaka, Virupaksha, and Vaishravana.
There are strong Chinese influences evident in the style of this thangka, from the landscape to the use of color and dry line. Its composition and color follow a set originally commissioned by the Yongle Emperor in the early 15th century, which was then copied numerous times in subsequent centuries. Based on the specific coloring, it may also in turn be following versions made during the 16th and 17th century. At the same time, the iconography references Tibetan tradition, particularly in the image of White Tara at the top center of the thangka, and Vanavasin's appearance with flywhisk and pointing gesture follows the description set forth in a Tibetan verse.
aic:147005.title: Arhat Vanavasin, One of the Sixteen Great Arhats, from a Set of Twenty-Three

aic:241750.texto: Gu Jianlong completed this portrait after he became a court painter or “painter-in-waiting” for Emperor Shunzhi (reigned 1644–61) at the royal palace in Beijing. In its attention to fine detail, this portrait reflects the opulence of Gu’s surroundings at court. His sitter, a Manchu prince, sits on a gold lacquer chair wearing a blue court robe embroidered with a large four-clawed dragon on the chest; on the robe’s skirt, small dragons race over multicolored waves, clouds, water. His red hat has a gold filigree ornament studded with pearls and a large ruby finial. He looks directly at the viewer, holding his necklace of coral and large crystal beads delicately in his left hand. In contrast to the garment rendered with bold outlines and vibrant colors, the facial features, including individual characteristics such as angular eyebrows, a broad nose, and gray hair, are subtly shaped through multiple layers of muted color washes. Gu also incorporated Western methods such as shading to carefully depict the sitter’s face and enhance the lifelike appearance.
aic:241750.title: Portrait of an Official

cma:147927.texto:
Monk Yuanzhao, with the honorific title Dazhi Lüshi, Great Wisdom Master of Vinaya, is depicted here as an itinerant monk, holding his alms bowl in the left and staff in the right. In 1142, Emperor Gaozong had bestowed Yuanzhao with a posthumous title, mentioned in the inscription, which suggests that the portrait was made after the master’s death. A master of the Lü sect of Buddhism, with a calm benevolent smile on his face, Yuanzhao was active on Mount Tiantai and in Hangzhou. Later, Liu Tao, a southerner from Changxing, added the inscription. 

The eulogy reads: 
Dignified he is, perfect in his upasampada [ordination of a monk]. His appearance is like his mind. Uncompromising and aloof. His mind is like his appearance. To say he is square, he proves to be round. He looks timid, yet his spirit is unbound. Having no attachment, and holding no reins, men and deities alike take refuge in him. —translated by Wai-Kam Ho
cma:147927.title: Portrait of Priest Dazhi (1048–1116), Master of Law

cma:147927.texto: A native of Hangzhou, the priest Dazhi was known for his eloquent exposition of Buddhist doctrines and for his success in winning many converts.
cma:147927.title: Portrait of Priest Dazhi (1048–1116), Master of Law

cma:151007.texto: This is a portrait study of the monk Seigen (1162–1231). The inscription identifies him and notes that the study is after a portrait in the subtemple Jizō’in at Daigoji. The artist included scars from an illness, and made notations about the colors the clothing should be. Seigen was abbot of Daigoji, one of the most influential Esoteric Buddhist temples in Japanese history.
cma:151007.title: Portrait Study of Seigen

cma:161268.texto:
The quest of capturing one’s spirit through imagery held a special place in the tradition of portrait making in East Asia. A portrait’s resemblance to the subject was considered to be a way to transmit the sitter’s spirit to the viewer. A three-quarter view, much preferred in Joseon-period portraits like this one, allows the viewer to examine the sitter’s personality or spirit without an exchange of glances. 

Dressed in a pale pink court uniform, the gentleman sits on a chair draped with leopard skin, a symbol of royal favor. Due to the missing inscription, which was likely trimmed off, we cannot identify him. Yet, we know a few things: His uniform informs us that he worked in the royal court sometime during the 1700s or later because the color of office uniforms changed from dark green to pale pink in the early 1700s. Considered to be an important historical family relic, this type of full-length portrait was often placed above the spirit house and venerated during ancestral worship rituals.
cma:161268.title: Portrait of an Official

cma:161268.texto: A piece of leopard skin covering the chair is a typical gift from the royal court to court officials.
cma:161268.title: Portrait of an Official

4. **Arhat Vanavasin, One of the Sixteen Great Arhats, from a Set of Twenty-Three**
   Tibeto-Chinese · late 17th/early 18th century · Pigment and gold on silk and cotton · Himalayan
   Ficha oficial: https://www.artic.edu/artworks/147005

   La obra utiliza colores verdes y azules en la vegetación y el paisaje, que son tonos fríos. [1]
   Aunque la obra tiene tonos fríos en el fondo, el retrato en sí es una figura religiosa con colores variados y no es un retrato tradicional de una persona específica.
   No es un retrato en el sentido clásico ni una versión en tonos fríos de un retrato específico.

   **Fuentes**
   [1] “This thangka most likely depicts the Arhat Vanavasin. He is seated amidst mountains facing slightly right with a flywhisk in his left hand and his right making a pointing gesture, just as he is described in certain Tibetan liturgical verses. He is surrounded by lush green and blue foliage, and seated beneath a small floating image of White Tara above. Tara appears peaceful, seated on a lotus, with one face and two hands, and holds a lotus with her left hand while making the boon-granting gesture (varada mudra) with her right.
The Sixteen Arhats were legendary early Indian disciples of the Buddha Shakyamuni. Although they were not worshipped individually and emerged relatively late as an iconographic group, they became a popular subject in Buddhist art in both Tibet and East Asia. The complete group usually consists of twenty-five figures: the sixteen arhats, the Buddha Shakyamuni, his two attendants Shariputra and Maudgalyayana, the Chinese monk devotee Hvashang and the lay upasaka Dharmatala, and the Four Great King of the cardinal directions, Dhritarashtra, Virudhaka, Virupaksha, and Vaishravana.
There are strong Chinese influences evident in the style of this thangka, from the landscape to the use of color and dry line. Its composition and color follow a set originally commissioned by the Yongle Emperor in the early 15th century, which was then copied numerous times in subsequent centuries. Based on the specific coloring, it may also in turn be following versions made during the 16th and 17th century. At the same time, the iconography references Tibetan tradition, particularly in the image of White Tara at the top center of the thangka, and Vanavasin's appearance with flywhisk and pointing gesture follows the description set forth in a Tibetan verse.”
       https://www.artic.edu/artworks/147005 · CC BY 4.0

A master of the Lü sect of Buddhism, with a calm benevolent smile on his face, Yuanzhao was active on Mount Tiantai and in Hangzhou. Later, Liu Tao, a southerner from Changxing, added the inscription.
